claim: The Johnston's organ (JO) is an antennal mechanosensory chordotonal organ in Drosophila melanogaster that elicits grooming of the antennae.
source: We previously discovered that grooming of the Drosophila melanogaster antennae is elicited by an antennal mechanosensory chordotonal organ, the Johnston's organ (JO) (Hampel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Hampel et al., 2015).

claim: JO mechanosensory neuron subpopulations project to different, discrete zones in the brain.
source: We show that the subpopulations project to different, discrete zones in the brain and differ in their responses to mechanical stimulation of the antennae.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing anatomical projections.

claim: JO mechanosensory neuron subpopulations differ in their responses to mechanical stimulation of the antennae.
source: We show that the subpopulations project to different, discrete zones in the brain and differ in their responses to mechanical stimulation of the antennae.
evidence: The claim is supported by physiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of each JO subpopulation elicits antennal grooming.
source: Although activation of each subpopulation elicits antennal grooming, distinct subpopulations also elicit the additional behaviors of wing flapping or backward locomotion.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Distinct JO subpopulations elicit the additional behaviors of wing flapping or backward locomotion.
source: Although activation of each subpopulation elicits antennal grooming, distinct subpopulations also elicit the additional behaviors of wing flapping or backward locomotion.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from optogenetic experiments.

claim: Mechanosensory neurons display diverse tuning to mechanical stimuli and differ widely in their peripheral and central nervous system (CNS) projections.
source: These neurons display diverse tuning to mechanical stimuli and differ widely in their peripheral and central nervous system (CNS) projections (Abraira and Ginty, 2013; Tuthill and Wilson, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mechanosensory neuron axonal projections from the body periphery terminate in an orderly topographical arrangement in discrete zones of the CNS.
source: One defining feature of mechanosensory neurons is that their axonal projections from the body periphery terminate in an orderly topographical arrangement in discrete zones of the CNS.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mechanosensory neurons.

claim: Different types of topographical organization are described across the diversity of mechanosensory neuron types based on features such as their responses to particular frequencies of sound (tonotopy) or their locations across the body (somatotopy).
source: Different types of topographical organization are described across the diversity of mechanosensory neuron types based on features such as their responses to particular frequencies of sound (tonotopy) or their locations across the body (somatotopy) (Appler and Goodrich, 2011; Erzurumlu et al., 2010; Muniak et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Topographical organization is thought to provide a means by which sensory neurons connect with the appropriate neural circuits in the CNS that facilitate relevant behavioral responses.
source: Although topographical organization is thought to provide a means by which sensory neurons connect with the appropriate neural circuits in the CNS that facilitate relevant behavioral responses (Kaas, 1997; Thivierge and Marcus, 2007), it remains unclear how sensory topography interfaces with the CNS behavioral circuitry.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature and represents a hypothesis in the field.

claim: It remains unclear how sensory topography interfaces with the CNS behavioral circuitry.
source: Although topographical organization is thought to provide a means by which sensory neurons connect with the appropriate neural circuits in the CNS that facilitate relevant behavioral responses (Kaas, 1997; Thivierge and Marcus, 2007), it remains unclear how sensory topography interfaces with the CNS behavioral circuitry.
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The JO detects diverse types of mechanical forces that move the antennae, including sound, wind, gravity, wing beats, and tactile displacements.
source: The JO detects diverse types of mechanical forces that move the antennae, including sound, wind, gravity, wing beats, and tactile displacements (Hampel et al., 2015; Ishikawa et al., 2017; Kamikouchi et al., 2009; Mamiya and Dickinson, 2015; Matsuo et al., 2014; Patella and Wilson, 2018; Yorozu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The JO contains about 480 mechanosensory neurons called JONs.
source: The ability of the JO to respond to these different stimuli is conferred by about 480 mechanosensory neurons called JONs (Kamikouchi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Subpopulations of JONs are selectively excited by different vibrational frequencies or by sustained displacements of the antennae and send their projections into discrete zones in the CNS.
source: Subpopulations of JONs are selectively excited by different vibrational frequencies or by sustained displacements of the antennae and send their projections into discrete zones in the CNS (Kamikouchi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The JONs are implicated in controlling diverse behaviors including courtship, locomotion, gravitaxis, wind-guided orientation, escape, flight, and grooming.
source: In accordance with their diverse physiological tuning properties, the JONs are implicated in controlling diverse behaviors including courtship, locomotion, gravitaxis, wind-guided orientation, escape, flight, and grooming (Hampel et al., 2015; Kamikouchi et al., 2009; Lehnert et al., 2013; Mamiya et al., 2011; Mamiya and Dickinson, 2015; Suver et al., 2019; Tootoonian et al., 2012; Vaughan et al., 2014; Yorozu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Efforts to define how the different JONs interface with downstream neural circuitry to influence behaviors have been hampered by the incomplete description of the morphologically heterogeneous JON types within each subpopulation.
source: However, efforts to define how the different JONs interface with downstream neural circuitry to influence these behaviors have been hampered by the incomplete description of the morphologically heterogeneous JON types within each subpopulation (Kamikouchi et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim identifies a limitation in previous research and is supported by citations.

claim: Activation of different JON subpopulations elicits antennal grooming behavior.
source: We previously discovered that activation of different JON subpopulations elicits antennal grooming behavior (Hampel et al., 2015), which involves the grasping and brushing of the antennae by the front legs (Böröczky et al., 2013; Robinson, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Antennal grooming involves the grasping and brushing of the antennae by the front legs.
source: We previously discovered that activation of different JON subpopulations elicits antennal grooming behavior (Hampel et al., 2015), which involves the grasping and brushing of the antennae by the front legs (Böröczky et al., 2013; Robinson, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 104 out of 147 reconstructed JONs were completely reconstructed, including all of their pre- and post-synaptic sites.
source: 70 JONs were manually reconstructed to completion, including all of their pre- and post-synaptic sites. We then reconstructed 77 additional JONs by assembling fragments created by the automated segmentation algorithm. 34 of these JONs were proofread using previously published methods (Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016), and traced to completion. Thus, out of the 147 reconstructed JONs, 104 (71%) were completely reconstructed with their entire morphology and all pre- and post-synaptic sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the EM reconstruction process.

claim: The projections of the different reconstructed JON subpopulations form a topographical map that resembles the one obtained from light-level anatomical analysis.
source: Thus, the projections of the different reconstructed JON subpopulations form a topographical map that resembles the one obtained from light-level anatomical analysis (Hampel et al., 2015; Kamikouchi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of EM data with previous light microscopy studies.

claim: The synapses of the 104 completely reconstructed JONs were distributed throughout the posterior regions of their respective zones.
source: We found that the synapses of the 104 completely reconstructed JONs were also distributed throughout the posterior regions of their respective zones (Figure 1H–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM data and references to figures.

claim: The subareas of each zone had both pre- and post-synaptic sites.
source: Examination of the total distribution of synapses did not reveal any clear difference, as the subareas of each zone had both pre- and post-synaptic sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM data and references to figures.

claim: JONs in these subareas can interface with downstream neurons.
source: Thus, JONs in these subareas can interface with downstream neurons, but they are likely also subject to regulation by other neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the presence of presynaptic sites in the subareas.

claim: JONs in these subareas are likely also subject to regulation by other neurons.
source: Thus, JONs in these subareas can interface with downstream neurons, but they are likely also subject to regulation by other neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the presence of postsynaptic sites in the subareas.

claim: The reconstructed JO-C, -D, -E, and -F neurons could be categorized into different types based on morphological similarity.
source: We visually inspected the reconstructed JO-C, -D, -E, and -F neurons and found that they could be categorized into different types based on morphological similarity (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual inspection of EM data and references to figures.

claim: The reconstructed JO-mz neurons showed no morphological similarity and could not be categorized.
source: However, the reconstructed JO-mz neurons showed no such similarity and could not be categorized (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual inspection of EM data and references to figures.

claim: The NBLAST clustering algorithm clustered most of the same JONs that were assigned as specific types by manual annotation.
source: In agreement with our manual annotations, the algorithm clustered most of the same JONs that we had assigned as specific types (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of manual and algorithmic categorization methods.

claim: The nine reconstructed JO-C neurons form the CM, CL, and CA subareas of zone C.
source: The nine reconstructed JO-C neurons form the CM, CL, and CA subareas of zone C.
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data.

claim: The nine reconstructed JO-C neurons were categorized into three morphologically distinct types that project to the CM, CL, and CA subareas (named JO-CM, -CL, and -CA neurons).
source: These neurons were categorized into three morphologically distinct types that project to these subareas (named JO-CM, -CL, and -CA neurons, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data and references to figures.

claim: The nine reconstructed JO-D neurons were categorized as two different types that form the AA, BI/BO, and DP subareas (named JO-DP and -DA neurons).
source: The nine reconstructed JO-D neurons were categorized as two different types that form the AA, BI/BO, and DP subareas (named JO-DP and -DA neurons, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data and references to figures.

claim: The 62 reconstructed JO-E neurons were categorized into seven types that form the EDC, EDM, EDP, EVM, EVP, EVL, and EV subareas (named JO-EDC, -EDM, -EDP, -EVM, -EVP, -EVL, and -EV neurons).
source: The 62 reconstructed JO-E neurons were categorized into seven types that form the EDC, EDM, EDP, EVM, EVP, EVL, and EV subareas (named JO-EDC, -EDM, -EDP, -EVM, -EVP, -EVL, and -EV neurons, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data and references to figures.

claim: The 60 reconstructed JO-F neurons were categorized into five types that form the FVA, FDA, FDP, FDL, and FVP subareas (named JO-FVA, -FDA, -FDP, -FDL, and -FVL neurons).
source: Lastly, the 60 reconstructed JO-F neurons were categorized into five types that form the FVA, FDA, FDP, FDL, and FVP subareas (named JO-FVA, -FDA, -FDP, -FDL, and -FVL neurons, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data and references to figures.

claim: JONs make synaptic connections with each other.
source: Analysis of all-to-all connectivity among the different reconstructed JONs revealed that they make synaptic connections with each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by connectivity analysis of EM data.

claim: The connectivity among JONs tended to occur most frequently among JONs that belonged to the same subpopulation.
source: Furthermore, the connectivity tended to occur most frequently among JONs that belonged to the same subpopulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 7, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by connectivity analysis of EM data and references to figures.

claim: JO-F neurons had numerous connections with each other but showed virtually no connectivity with JO-C or -E neurons.
source: For example, the JO-F neurons had numerous connections with each other but showed virtually no connectivity with JO-C or -E neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by connectivity analysis of EM data.

claim: JONs that project to the same zones show synaptic connectivity, while JONs projecting to different zones show little or no connectivity.
source: Thus, JONs that project to the same zones show synaptic connectivity, while JONs projecting to different zones show little or no connectivity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the connectivity analysis of EM data.

claim: Four different driver lines were produced that expressed in JONs whose activation could elicit antennal grooming.
source: We used a Split GAL4 (spGAL4) screening approach to produce four different lines that expressed in JONs whose activation could elicit antennal grooming (see Materials and methods for details, Figure 3A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the spGAL4 screening and references to figures.

claim: Two of the identified drivers express in both JO-C and -E neurons and were named JO-C/E-1 and JO-C/E-2.
source: Two of the identified drivers express in both JO-C and -E neurons and were named JO-C/E-1 (spGAL4 combination: VT005525-AD ∩ R27H08-DBD) and JO-C/E-2 (R39H04-AD ∩ R27H08-DBD) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis of driver line expression patterns and references to figures.

claim: Two driver lines express mainly in JO-F neurons and were named JO-F-1 and JO-F-2.
source: The other two lines express mainly in JO-F neurons and were named JO-F-1 (R25F11-AD ∩ R27H08-DBD) and JO-F-2 (VT050231-AD ∩ R27H08-DBD) (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis of driver line expression patterns and references to figures.

claim: Analysis of all four driver lines revealed no evidence of JO-A, -B, -D, or -mz neurons in their expression patterns.
source: Our analysis of all four driver lines revealed no evidence of JO-A, -B, -D, or -mz neurons in their expression patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis of driver line expression patterns.

claim: Both JO-C/E-1 and JO-C/E-2 lines express in JONs projecting to the subareas CL, EDP, EVP, EDM, EDC, and EVM.
source: Both lines express in JONs projecting to the subareas CL, EDP, EVP, EDM, EDC, and EVM.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of driver line expression patterns with EM reconstructions.

claim: Both JO-C/E-1 and JO-C/E-2 lines express in JO-CL, -EDC, -EDM, -EDP, -EVM, and -EVP neurons.
source: Because each subarea is formed by specific JON types (Figure 2B), we could deduce that both lines express in JO-CL, -EDC, -EDM, -EDP, -EVM, and -EVP neurons (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the subareas targeted by the driver lines and the JON types that form those subareas.

claim: Neither JO-C/E-1 nor JO-C/E-2 expresses in JO-F neurons.
source: Importantly, neither line expresses in JO-F neurons as there are no ventral-projecting JONs in their patterns (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis of driver line expression patterns and references to figures.

claim: The JO-C/E-1 and −2 driver lines express specifically in JO-C and -E neurons.
source: We concluded that the JO-C/E-1 and −2 driver lines express specifically in JO-C and -E neurons (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis of driver line expression patterns and references to figures.

claim: Both JO-F-1 and JO-F-2 lines express in JONs projecting to each zone F subarea.
source: The JO-F-1 and −2 driver lines express in JONs projecting to each zone F subarea (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis of driver line expression patterns and references to figures.

claim: Both JO-F-1 and JO-F-2 lines express in JO-FVA, -FDL, -FVL, -FDA, and -FDP neurons.
source: Based on the EM-reconstructed JON types that form each subarea (Figure 2B), we predicted that both lines would express in JO-FVA, -FDL, -FVL, -FDA, and -FDP neurons (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the subareas targeted by the driver lines and the JON types that form those subareas.

claim: JO-F-1 and JO-F-2 lines also express in JO-EVP neurons.
source: A portion of the labeled JONs projected to zone E and had a posterior projection, leading us to propose they are JO-EVP neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by MCFO data and references to figures.

claim: JO-F-1 and −2 express mostly in JO-F neurons, but also in JO-EVP neurons.
source: We concluded that JO-F-1 and −2 express mostly in JO-F neurons, but also in JO-EVP neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis of driver line expression patterns.

claim: JO-F-1 and −2 appear to express in the same JON types as the previously reported JO-F driver line named aJO-spGAL4-1.
source: Of note, JO-F-1 and −2 appear to express in the same JON types as our previously reported JO-F driver line named aJO-spGAL4-1 (Hampel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous work.

claim: The morphology of the aligned projections of JO-C/E and -F driver lines was very similar to the EM-reconstructed JO-C/E and -F neurons.
source: Further, the morphology of the aligned projections was very similar to the EM-reconstructed JO-C/E and -F neurons (Figure 3H,I, right panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of light microscopy and EM data and references to figures.

claim: Expression of GFP under control of JO-C/E-1 and −2 labeled JON cell bodies in a ring around the JO bowl.
source: Expression of GFP under control of JO-C/E-1 and −2 labeled JON cell bodies in a ring around the JO bowl (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data and references to figures.

claim: JO-C/E-1 and −2 showed only sparse expression around the anterior dorsal (A-D) portion of the bowl.
source: In contrast to the previously published JO-C/E drivers that showed expression around the entire ring of the JO bowl (Kamikouchi et al., 2006), JO-C/E-1 and −2 showed only sparse expression around the anterior dorsal (A-D) portion of the bowl (Figure 4C',D').
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data and references to figures.

claim: JO-F-1 and −2 showed expression in two clusters in the dorsal and ventral regions of the JO bowl.
source: JO-F-1 and −2 showed expression in two clusters in the dorsal and ventral regions of the JO bowl (Figure 4E,F), in agreement with our previous results (Hampel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data and references to figures.

claim: The dorsal expression of JO-F-1 and −2 was in the anterior and posterior regions of the bowl (A-D and P-D), while the ventral expression was largely restricted to the posterior (P-V) region.
source: The dorsal expression was in the anterior and posterior regions of the bowl (A-D and P-D), while the ventral expression was largely restricted to the posterior (P-V) region (Figure 4E',F').
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data and references to figures.

claim: JO-F-1 and −2 expression was not restricted to the dorsal and ventral clusters, but was also in more intermediate JONs in the posterior part of the bowl.
source: In contrast to what we previously reported, JO-F-1 and −2 expression was not restricted to the dorsal and ventral clusters, but was also in more intermediate JONs in the posterior part of the bowl.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data.

claim: The JONs targeted by the JO-C/E and -F driver lines occupy common (P-D and P-V) and distinct (A-D [JO-F] and A-V [JO-C/E]) regions of the JO bowl.
source: A comparison of the distributions of JONs that are targeted by the JO-C/E and -F driver lines revealed that they occupy common (P-D and P-V) and distinct (A-D [JO-F] and A-V [JO-C/E]) regions of the JO bowl (Figure 4B'–F').
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data and references to figures.

claim: The JONs labeled by the JO-C/E-1 and −2 driver lines showed increased GCaMP6f fluorescence in response to both push and pull of the arista.
source: In accord with this finding, the JONs labeled by the JO-C/E-1 and −2 driver lines showed increased GCaMP6f fluorescence in response to both push and pull of the arista (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data and references to figures.

claim: The fluorescence increase of the JO-C/E-1-labeled neurons in response to antennal pushes was lower than that of the JO-C/E-2-labeled neurons.
source: Notably, the fluorescence increase of the JO-C/E-1-labeled neurons in response to antennal pushes was lower than that of the JO-C/E-2-labeled neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: The different responses of JO-C/E-1 and JO-C/E-2 labeled neurons may indicate that the lines express in different ratios of JO-C and -E neuron types that are known to differentially respond to antennal pushes (JO-C neurons) or pulls (JO-E neurons).
source: Although both driver lines express in the same neuron types (Figure 3G), these different responses may indicate that the lines express in different ratios of JO-C and -E neuron types that are known to differentially respond to antennal pushes (JO-C neurons) or pulls (JO-E neurons) (Kamikouchi et al., 2009; Patella and Wilson, 2018; Yorozu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the different responses and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There was no evidence that the JO-C/E neurons responded to vibrations.
source: Also in agreement with previous results using the immobilized fly preparation (Kamikouchi et al., 2009; Matsuo et al., 2014; Yorozu et al., 2009), we found no evidence that the JO-C/E neurons responded to vibrations (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—figure supplements 1A–D, 200 Hz test shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data and references to figures.

claim: The JONs that are labeled by JO-F-1 or −2 did not respond to push or pull movements of the antennae.
source: Under the experimental conditions used here, the JONs that are labeled by JO-F-1 or −2 did not respond to push or pull movements of the antennae (Figure 5D,E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data and references to figures.

claim: A vibration frequency that could evoke a response in JO-F neurons could not be identified, including low (40 Hz), middle (200 Hz), and high frequency vibrations (400 and 800 Hz).
source: Furthermore, we could not identify a vibration frequency that could evoke a response in these JONs, including low (40 Hz, N = 2 flies), middle (200 Hz, N = 10 flies), and high frequency vibrations (400 and 800 Hz, N = 2 flies) (Figure 5D,E, Figure 5—figure supplements 2A–D, 200 Hz test shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data and references to figures.

claim: It remains to be determined what stimulus excites JO-F neurons.
source: Thus, it remains to be determined what stimulus excites these JONs (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: JO-C/E and -F neurons do not show similar responses to mechanical stimuli in immobilized flies.
source: However, our results indicate that JO-C/E and -F neurons do not show similar responses to mechanical stimuli in immobilized flies.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: JO-C/E and -F neurons are both anatomically and physiologically distinct from each other.
source: Thus, these different JON subpopulations are both anatomically and physiologically distinct from each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical and physiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of either JO-C/E or -F neurons elicits grooming.
source: We first reproduced our previous results by showing that activation of either JO-C/E or -F neurons elicits grooming (Figure 6A, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments and references to figures and videos.

claim: A driver line named JO-F-3 (R60E02-LexA) expresses exclusively in JO-F neurons and elicited grooming in the activation experiment when driving CsChrimson.
source: To address this possibility, we identified another driver line named JO-F-3 (R60E02-LexA) that expresses exclusively in JO-F neurons and elicited grooming in the activation experiment when driving CsChrimson (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments and references to figures.

claim: The data further implicate the JO-C/E and -F neurons in antennal grooming.
source: Thus, the data presented here further implicate the JO-C/E and -F neurons in antennal grooming.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: It remains unclear whether one or both of JO-C and -E subpopulations is responsible for the grooming.
source: However, because the JO-C/E driver lines express in both JO-C and -E neurons, it remains unclear whether one or both of these subpopulations is responsible for the grooming.
evidence: The claim identifies a limitation of the current study.

claim: Five-second optogenetic stimulation of the JO-C/E neurons elicited grooming that lasted throughout the duration of the stimulus.
source: Five-second optogenetic stimulation of the JO-C/E neurons elicited grooming that lasted throughout the duration of the stimulus.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: The JO-F neurons elicited shorter duration grooming that terminated prior to stimulus cessation.
source: In contrast, the JO-F neurons elicited shorter duration grooming that terminated prior to stimulus cessation.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: The distinct grooming durations were due to the physiological properties and/or functional circuit connectivity of each JON subpopulation.
source: This suggests that the distinct grooming durations were due to the physiological properties and/or functional circuit connectivity of each JON subpopulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the number of labeled JONs did not differ markedly between the lines.

claim: Activation of the JO-C/E neurons elicited flies simultaneously grooming and performing wing flapping movements.
source: In the case in which we activated the JO-C/E neurons, the flies were observed simultaneously grooming and performing wing flapping movements (Figure 6B–D, JO-C/E-1 and −2, gray trace, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments and references to figures and videos.

claim: Activation of JO-F neurons elicited a backward locomotor response that appeared as if flies were avoiding an object that bumped into their antennae.
source: In contrast, activation of JO-F neurons elicited a backward locomotor response that appeared as if flies were avoiding an object that bumped into their antennae (Video 3, Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments and references to figures and videos.

claim: The backward locomotion and grooming elicited by JO-F neuron activation were sequential and mutually exclusive.
source: The backward locomotion and grooming were sequential and mutually exclusive, as the locomotion occurred briefly at the onset of the stimulus and was immediately followed by grooming (Figure 6B,C, JO-F-1 and −2, black and magenta traces).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments and references to figures.

claim: Control flies also showed backward locomotion in response to the red-light stimulus.
source: Control flies also showed backward locomotion in response to the red-light stimulus (Figure 6B,C, control, black trace, Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments and references to figures and videos.

claim: Less than half of control flies responded with backward locomotion (42%), whereas nearly all of the JO-F neuron activation flies showed backward locomotion (97% for JO-F-1, 100% for JO-F-2).
source: However, less than half of these flies responded (42%), whereas nearly all of the JO-F neuron activation flies showed backward locomotion (97% for JO-F-1, 100% for JO-F-2).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: JO-F neuron activation elicited longer-lasting backward locomotion than controls, with the experimental flies spending between 5- and 8-fold more time in backward locomotion than control flies.
source: JO-F neuron activation also elicited longer-lasting backward locomotion than controls, with the experimental flies spending between 5- and 8-fold more time in backward locomotion than control flies (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments and references to figures.

claim: The JO-C/E and -F neurons are anatomically and physiologically distinct subpopulations that elicit both common and distinct behaviors.
source: Taken together, our results reveal that the JO-C/E and -F neurons are anatomically and physiologically distinct subpopulations that elicit both common and distinct behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical, physiological, and behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A recent study used a serial-section EM volume of the adult fruit fly brain to reconstruct a major portion of the JO-A and -B neurons.
source: A recent study used a serial-section EM volume of the adult fruit fly brain to reconstruct a major portion of the JO-A and -B neurons, demonstrating the utility of this approach for defining JON diversity (Kim et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It was previously estimated that there are about 200 JO-C and -E neurons total.
source: However, it was previously estimated that there are about 200 JO-C and -E neurons total (Kamikouchi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: 36% of the JO-C and -E neurons were reconstructed (71 reconstructed out of 200).
source: This suggests that we reconstructed 36% of the JO-C and -E neurons (71 reconstructed out of 200).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the estimated total number of JO-C and -E neurons and the number reconstructed.

claim: The EM-reconstructed JONs represent the major diversity of the JO-C, -D, -E, and -F neurons.
source: Two lines of evidence suggested that the EM-reconstructed JONs represent the major diversity of the JO-C, -D, -E, and -F neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that all previously described subareas were observed and that JONs could be categorized based on morphological similarities.

claim: The reconstructions provide the most comprehensive description of the JO-C, -D, -E, -F, and -mz neurons to date.
